Analytic equations and characteristic directions

An analytic differential equation determines every noncharacteristic singular direction of its solution from the corresponding direction of its right-hand side. The estimate holds for the analytic wavefront set and for every derivative-growth scale considered here. Its support consequences are stronger than ellipticity: Poisson brackets can rule out the end of a solution's support even when characteristic covectors remain.

We use Derivative growth and finite-order localization, especially its analytic derivative bounds, controlled cutoffs and bounded-distribution criterion; Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 3–4 and 7; Both analytic directions at support boundaries, Theorem 1, Corollary 2 and Proposition 3; and Characteristic motion and closed-set barriers, Corollary 5. Fourier inversion and finite-order pairings have their proofs in the supplied Fourier foundation, F1–F5, and convolution lesson, B0–B2. The calculus and integration foundations supply compactness, Leibniz' rule, convergent power series and the integrals below.

5. Where a solution's support can end

For a relatively closed , write , with closure in the punctured cotangent space and the minus sign changing only the covector. The support-boundary lesson proves , including complex distributions.

Corollary 4 (Holmgren uniqueness). If has analytic coefficients and , then

Consequently, if vanishes on one side of a hypersurface near , and its nonzero normal at is noncharacteristic, then vanishes on a neighborhood of . If is elliptic and connected, vanishing on one nonempty open subset implies throughout .

Proof. Apply Theorem 3 with and , then the support-boundary inclusion. For the surface statement, if belonged to the support, a defining function with the appropriate sign would be a supporting function for that support. The support-boundary lesson, Proposition 3, puts its nonzero differential in the closure of the actual exterior normal set. This contradicts (24). Hence is outside the support, which is precisely neighborhood vanishing. In the elliptic case, (24) leaves no normal. Every boundary point of a closed support has a limiting nonzero normal, by that same proposition. The support thus has no relative boundary and is both open and closed. Connectedness and the nonempty open zero set force it to be empty.

Theorem 5 (the bracket test for support uniqueness). Let be the smallest collection of smooth functions on containing every smooth function vanishing on , and closed under the bracket . If , every member of vanishes on . If these functions have no common zero, a solution on connected vanishing on a nonempty open set is identically zero. For a one-sided zero set along a surface, neighborhood vanishing holds whenever at least one member is nonzero at the marked normal.

Proof. Put . Corollary 5 of the characteristic-motion lesson says that smooth functions vanishing on are closed under Poisson brackets. The same holds for : for the antipodal map , the coordinate chain rule gives

Apply the actual-normal result to the two pullbacks. Intersecting these two vanishing classes and then using continuity proves bracket closure of the functions vanishing on . By (24), this class contains all generators defining , so it contains their smallest bracket-closed collection. The last two assertions now follow from the limiting normal at any support boundary and the supporting-normal argument in Corollary 4. This proves the test for the whole normal closure, not only the actual exterior normals.

Mathematical sources

Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, second edition, 2003 reprint, §8.6, Theorems 8.6.1, 8.6.5 and 8.6.6, Lemmas 8.6.2–8.6.4, and the two following examples (edition). The exposition uses a finite weighted-seminorm proof for the ordered derivative estimate and supplies the full transpose, frequency split and support arguments. The characteristic-half-space converse is a separate theorem and is not asserted here.
